planting.note: Scarify stored seed with sandpaper or a hot-water soak, then direct-sow in fall into the leanest, fastest-draining soil available; avoid phosphorus-heavy fertilizer, which disrupts its nitrogen-fixing rhizobial partnership.

directions: Famous as the first vascular plant to recolonize the Mount St. Helens pumice plain after the 1980 eruption, this extremely tough low-growing lupine tolerates nutrient-poor, droughty mineral soils better than almost any other garden plant. It is a nitrogen-fixer and larval host for several blue butterflies. Give it the leanest, fastest-draining soil available — rich garden loam actually shortens its life and reduces flowering.

planting.note: Direct-sow or use deep plug trays rather than transplanting bare-root seedlings, since the taproot resents disturbance; scarify or hot-water-treat stored seed for even germination.

directions: A robust Intermountain West perennial for dry meadow and xeric border plantings east of the Cascades, this lupine's silvery-silky foliage provides season-long textural interest even before bloom. Site it in open, well-drained slopes mimicking its sagebrush-steppe origin — heavy irrigation or clay soil invites root rot. Once established it is long-lived and self-sows modestly without becoming aggressive.

planting.note: Direct-sow outdoors in fall to let natural freeze-thaw cycles substitute for manual scarification, into sharply drained soil with minimal summer water.

directions: Distinctive among western lupines for the small spur projecting from its flower's calyx, this species forms neat erect clumps of silvery-haired foliage suited to high-elevation rock gardens and dry woodland-edge plantings. Native to dry, open sagebrush-steppe slopes between roughly 4,000 and 8,000 feet, it performs best with sharp drainage and minimal summer supplemental water once rooted in. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive beds, which shorten its lifespan.

planting.note: Direct-sow where it is to grow ahead of winter rains, since it resents transplanting like other desert annual lupines; scarify or hot-water-soak seed first.

directions: A fast, showy winter and spring annual for Sonoran and Mojave desert gardens and wildflower meadows, this lupine attracts large numbers of native bees and thrives in decomposed granite or sandy washes where little else blooms. After establishment, limit irrigation to at most twice a month — overwatering in summer, when the plant is naturally senescing, invites rot. It reseeds readily in sandy, fast-draining soil, so a single good bloom year can self-sustain a patch for seasons afterward.

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-soak stored seed and sow into loose, gritty, fast-draining sand replicating native dune and beach habitat; also spreads vegetatively by rhizome once established.

directions: A low, mat-forming coastal perennial useful for dune stabilization and sandy coastal gardens, this species is historically significant as a Pacific Northwest First Nations food plant — roasted, pounded roots were traded with the Lewis and Clark expedition at Fort Clatsop, giving it strong ethnobotanical-garden interest. Plant in loose, gritty, fast-draining sand; it struggles in heavy or poorly drained soil. Raw lupine tissue, especially seed, is alkaloid-bearing and should not be eaten unprocessed.

planting.note: Scarify seed or soak 12 hours in warm water, then fall-sow directly into lean, well-drained soil; does not transplant well once past the seedling stage.

directions: The most visually distinctive lupine on this list, this California-endemic annual combines pink, cream, and yellow simultaneously on the same raceme, unlike the typical blue or purple palette dominating the genus. Site in open, dry clearings or exposed slopes with light shade tolerance at woodland margins, mimicking its Sierra foothill forest-opening habitat. Because of its disjunct, patchy wild distribution across the Sierra Nevada, Transverse Ranges, and Santa Lucia Mountains, treat seed source carefully to preserve regional genetic distinctness if used in restoration contexts.

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-soak seed and fall-sow in drifts into fast-draining gravelly soil; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer, which produces leggy growth at the expense of flowering.

directions: A tall, fast-growing California-endemic annual forming erect racemes of vivid blue flowers, this species offers exceptional pollinator-support value, with documented support for well over 100 likely pollinator species. It needs fast-draining gravelly soil, as a wash and foothill-grassland native, and will rot in heavy clay or over-irrigated beds. Plant the long racemes in drifts rather than singly, both for visual impact and to maximize pollinator visitation.

planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-treat seed and sow in fall into open mountain, prairie, or plateau soil that is well-drained but not bone-dry; avoid late-day overhead watering, which promotes fungal issues in the hairy foliage.

directions: A large, robust Great Basin and Intermountain perennial with distinctive white-woolly, velvety foliage texture, this lupine contrasts well against the typically smoother-leaved lupines already in cultivation. Unlike several desert lupines, it tolerates and even prefers somewhat more moisture-retentive sites within its sagebrush-steppe range. Give it room — it is one of the larger-bodied Lupinus species and can overwhelm small rock-garden plantings.
